items.q: What is the average rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ from 0 s to 200 s? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the change in concentration. A rate is that change divided by the time: 0.066 M / 200 s.
Value: that is the rate of appearance of NO₂. The question asks how fast N₂O₅ disappears, so do not use the 4 : 2 ratio here.

items.q: Over the same interval, 0 s to 200 s, what is the average rate of appearance of NO₂? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: that is the rate for N₂O₅. Use the coefficients: 4 NO₂ form for every 2 N₂O₅ used, so NO₂ appears twice as fast.
Value: you divided by 2 instead of multiplying. NO₂ has the larger coefficient (4 vs 2), so it appears faster than N₂O₅ disappears.

items.q: The average rate of disappearance of N₂O₅ from 200 s to 400 s is smaller than from 0 s to 200 s. Which statement best explains this?
options: Less N₂O₅ is left per liter, so fewer molecules react each second
The NO₂ that forms slows the reaction by soaking up the remaining heat in the flask
The temperature of the flask falls as the reaction goes on
The flask is sealed, so the pressure stops more molecules from reacting

items.q: At the moment N₂O₅ is disappearing at 2.4 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, how fast is O₂ appearing?
Which claim about the two trials is supported by the graph and the setup?
options: The powder reacts faster at first: more of its surface touches the acid
The chips react faster at first, because large pieces carry many more particles into the acid
The powder reacts faster at the start, because powdered marble is a different compound
Both trials start at the same rate, because they use the same mass of marble

items.q: Both trials end at the same volume of CO₂. Which statement best explains why?
options: The same mass of CaCO₃, the limiting reactant, reacted in each trial
The acid ran out at the same moment in both trials
The powder reacted faster, so it should have made more gas, but some gas escaped
The rate of a reaction and the amount of product it makes are the same thing

items.q: Using the graph, what is the average rate of CO₂ production in trial 1 (chips) from 0 s to 60 s? Give your answer in mL/s.

mistakes.why: Value: the time interval is 60 s − 0 s = 60 s. Divide the volume collected by 60 s.
Value: you read the powder curve. Trial 1 is the chips.

items.q: Which change to trial 1 would make the CO₂ come off faster at the start without changing the final volume of CO₂?
options: Use 2.0 M HCl instead of 1.0 M HCl
Use 0.66 g of marble chips instead of 0.33 g
Use the same mass of marble in one single large lump
Add 50 mL of water to the acid before adding the chips

items.q: In the reaction N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) → 2 NH₃(g), hydrogen is used up at 0.090 M/s. At what rate, in M/s, does ammonia form?

mistakes.why: Value: you inverted the ratio. 2 NH₃ form for every 3 H₂ used, so multiply by 2/3, not 3/2.
Value: you used the coefficient of NH₃ alone. Compare it with the coefficient of H₂: the ratio is 2 : 3.

items.q: A reaction rate is reported as 3.0 × 10⁻³ M/s. What does this number describe?
options: The change in molarity of a substance each second
The number of moles of product made by the time the reaction is over
The energy given off per second by the reacting mixture
The time the reaction needs to reach completion

items.q: For 2 N₂O(g) → 2 N₂(g) + O₂(g), which expression gives the same rate whichever substance is measured?
options: −½ Δ[N₂O]/Δt = ½ Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt
−2 Δ[N₂O]/Δt = 2 Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt
Δ[N₂O]/Δt = Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt
−½ Δ[N₂O]/Δt = −½ Δ[N₂]/Δt = Δ[O₂]/Δt

items.q: A student reacts 1.0 g of zinc granules with excess hydrochloric acid, then repeats the experiment with 1.0 g of zinc powder. Predict how each quantity changes in the second run.

variables.name: Time for all the zinc to dissolve

items.q: A strip of magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid. Which changes would increase the rate of the reaction? Select all that apply.
options: Warming the acid before adding the magnesium
Using more concentrated hydrochloric acid
Pouring the same acid into a wider beaker
Adding water to the acid

items.q: On a graph of [reactant] against time, how do you find the instantaneous rate at t = 50 s?
options: Take the negative of the slope of the tangent at 50 s
Divide the concentration at 50 s by 50 s
Join the first and last points and take the slope of that line
Read the concentration at 50 s; that value is the rate

items.q: A colored reactant fades as it reacts, and a spectrophotometer records absorbance every 10 s. The absorbance falls by 0.080 in the first 10 s and by 0.030 between 60 s and 70 s. What can you conclude?
options: Faster at the start: absorbance is proportional to concentration
Faster near 60 s, because the solution is much less colored by then
The rates are not comparable, because absorbance is not a concentration
The rate is the same throughout, because the same solution is measured

items.q: Two students run the same reaction. Student X uses 0.10 M reactant and collects 25 mL of gas in 50 s. Student Y uses 0.20 M reactant and collects 50 mL of gas in 50 s. Student Y concludes, "My reaction made twice as much gas, so twice as much reactant reacted, but the rates are equal." What is the error?
options: Twice the gas in the same time is twice the rate
Y should have measured for twice as long before comparing
Gas volumes from different concentrations are not comparable
There is no error; the two rates are in fact equal to each other

items.q: A 0.250 L solution starts with 0.0800 mol of a dye. After 40.0 s, 0.0560 mol of the dye remains. What is the average rate of disappearance of the dye, in M/s?

mistakes.why: Value: you used moles, not molarity. Divide the moles by 0.250 L first, then by the time.
Value: use the change in concentration, not the amount left at the end.

items.q: What is the order of the reaction with respect to NO?
options: Zero order
First order
Second order
Third order

items.q: What is the order of the reaction with respect to Cl₂?
options: Zero order
Half order
First order
Second order

items.q: Using trial 1, calculate the rate constant k. Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you used [NO] to the first power. The rate law is second order in NO, so square it: (0.0100 M)².
Value: no factor of 2 belongs here. The rate law and k come from the measured rate directly, not from the coefficient of NOCl.

items.q: Predict the initial rate, in M/s, of a fourth trial with [NO] = 0.0300 M and [Cl₂] = 0.0050 M.

mistakes.why: Value: [NO] must be squared. The rate law is second order in NO.
Value: tripling [NO] multiplies the rate by 3² = 9, not 3.

items.q: A student says, "The coefficient of NO is 2 and of Cl₂ is 1, so I could have written the rate law without doing the experiment." Which response is best?
options: Orders come from data; here they happen to match the coefficients
The student is right: rate-law orders are the coefficients of the balanced equation
The orders match the coefficients of the products, not those of the reactants
For gas reactions like this one, coefficients give the orders

items.q: Which rate law agrees with the data?
options: rate = k[X]
rate = k[X][Y]
rate = k[Y]
rate = k[X]²

items.q: Y is still used up as the reaction goes. Which statement about Y is consistent with the data?
options: Y is used up, but its concentration does not set the rate
Y is not consumed by the reaction
Y is a product of the reaction, not a reactant
Y is a solid, so it has no concentration

items.q: Using the data for X, what is the first-order rate constant? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by [X][Y]. The rate law is rate = k[X], so divide by [X] only.

items.q: Predict the initial rate, in M/s, when [X] = 0.45 M and [Y] = 0.30 M.

mistakes.why: Value: [Y] does not appear in the rate law, so doubling [Y] does not change the rate.

items.q: For rate = k[A][B]², what are the units of k when concentrations are in M and time in s?
options: M s⁻¹
s⁻¹
M⁻¹ s⁻¹
M⁻² s⁻¹

items.q: For A + B → C, the rate is first order in B. When [A] and [B] are both doubled at the same time, the initial rate becomes 8 times larger. What is the order in A?
options: Zero order
First order
Second order
Third order

items.q: For the rate law rate = k[NO₂]², the concentration of NO₂ is doubled at constant temperature. Predict each change.
Which statements about a rate law are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The rate constant k changes when the temperature changes
The rate constant k changes when a concentration changes
The orders equal the coefficients in the overall balanced equation
The units of k are the same for each rate law

items.q: A reaction has rate = k[A]² with k = 0.62 M⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the rate, in M/s, when [A] = 0.040 M?

mistakes.why: Value: square the concentration. The rate law is second order in A.
Value: you doubled [A] instead of squaring it. (0.040)² = 0.0016, not 0.080.

items.q: A reaction is zero order in its only reactant. Which statement describes it?
options: Its rate stays the same as the reactant is used
Its rate doubles when the reactant concentration doubles
It does not start until a second reactant is added
Its rate constant has the units s⁻¹

items.q: A student wants to find the order in B for A + B → products. Which plan would work?
options: Vary [B] while holding [A] and temperature constant; compare initial rates
Run a single trial and read the order from the coefficient of B in the equation
Run trials that change both [A] and [B] together by the same factor
Run trials at several temperatures, keeping the same [A] and [B]

items.q: Which claim about the order of this reaction is best supported by the table?
options: First order: ln[C₃H₆] drops about 0.30 per 500 s
Second order: 1/[C₃H₆] goes up in each 500 s interval
Zero order: [C₃H₆] goes down in each 500 s interval
First order, because the graph of these data is linear

items.q: Use the first and last rows to find the rate constant k. Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you used log (base 10). The integrated rate law uses the natural log, ln.
Value: that slope comes from the 1/[A] column, the second-order plot. This reaction is first order, so use the ln[A] column.

items.q: With k = 6.0 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹, what is the half-life of cyclopropane at this temperature? Include units.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied. The half-life is t½ = 0.693 / k.
Value: t½ = 0.693/k; you left out the 0.693 (that is ln 2).

items.q: Predict [C₃H₆], in M, at 3000 s if the reaction continues the same way.

mistakes.why: Value: that is ln[A], not [A]. Finish by taking e to that power: [A] = e^(ln[A]).
Value: you used 10^(−kt). The first-order law uses e^(−kt) (natural log).

items.q: Which statement correctly uses the graph to find the order with respect to NO₂?
options: 1/[NO₂] vs time is linear, so second order
The plot is a straight line, so the reaction is zero order in NO₂
1/[NO₂] vs time is linear, so the reaction is first order in NO₂
The plot rises, so [NO₂] rises with time and NO₂ is a product here

items.q: Use the slope of the 1/[NO₂] line to find the second-order rate constant. Include units.

mistakes.why: Sign: for second order the slope of 1/[A] vs t is +k, and k is positive.
Value: the run is the whole time interval, 100 s − 0 s = 100 s. Slope = (75 − 25) M⁻¹ ÷ 100 s.

items.q: How long, in seconds, does it take for [NO₂] to fall from 0.0400 M to 0.0100 M?

mistakes.why: Value: you used the first-order half-life twice. This is second order: use 1/[A]t − 1/[A]₀ = kt.
Value: you multiplied by k. Solve for t: t = (1/[A]t − 1/[A]₀)/k.

items.q: How does the time for [NO₂] to halve change as the reaction goes on?
options: It gets longer, since the rate falls with [NO₂]²
It stays the same, since half-lives are constant for any reaction
It gets shorter, since there is less NO₂ left to react each time
It stays the same, since the rate constant k does not change

items.q: What is the order of this reaction with respect to NH₃, and what is the evidence?
options: Zero order: [NH₃] vs time is a straight line
First order: [NH₃] falls steadily with time
Second order: [NH₃] vs time slopes downward
Zero order: the rate drops to zero by the end

items.q: What is the rate constant k, from the slope of the line? Include units.

mistakes.why: Sign: the slope of [A] vs t is −k; k itself is positive.
Value: for zero order, k is the slope itself, not the slope divided by [A].

items.q: While [NH₃] falls at 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ M/s, at what rate does H₂ form, in M/s?

mistakes.why: Value: H₂ has a different coefficient. 3 H₂ form for every 2 NH₃ used, so multiply by 3/2.
Value: the ratio is inverted. H₂ (coefficient 3) forms faster than NH₃ (coefficient 2) is used.

items.q: The wire's surface has a fixed number of spots where NH₃ can sit and react. Which explanation of the zero-order behavior fits this?
options: The spots stay full, so a fixed number react per second
NH₃ molecules in the gas react with each other, away from the wire
The wire itself is used up at a steady rate, and that sets the rate
The NH₃ molecules in the gas react at the same instant

items.q: Iodine-131 decays by a first-order process with a half-life of 8.02 days. How many days pass until 12.5% of a sample is left?

mistakes.why: Value: two half-lives leave 25%. 100% → 50% → 25% → 12.5% is three half-lives.
Value: 12.5% is (½)³, so three half-lives, not eight.

items.q: A first-order reaction is run twice at the same temperature, the second time with twice the starting concentration. Predict each change in the second run.
A first-order reaction has k = 0.0350 min⁻¹. Starting at 0.800 M, what is [A] after 20.0 min, in M?

mistakes.why: Value: you used base 10. The first-order law is [A]t = [A]₀e^(−kt).
Value: that subtracts kt as if the reaction were zero order.

items.q: Which pair correctly matches a straight-line plot with its slope?
options: ln[A] vs t, first order; slope −k
1/[A] vs t, second order; slope −k
[A] vs t, first order; slope −k
ln[A] vs t, second order; slope +k

items.q: A first-order reaction has a half-life of 45 s. What is k, in s⁻¹?

mistakes.why: Value: rearrange t½ = 0.693/k to k = 0.693/t½, not t½/0.693.
Value: k = 0.693/t½; you left out ln 2 = 0.693.

items.q: What is the rate law for this elementary step?
options: rate = k[A][B]
rate = k[AB]
rate = k[A]²
rate = k[A] + k[B]

items.q: How does the initial rate in Box 2 compare with Box 1?
options: Half as fast
The same
Twice as fast
Four times as fast

items.q: How does the initial rate in Box 3 compare with Box 1?
options: The same
Twice as fast
Four times as fast
Eight times as fast

items.q: What is the molecularity of A + B → AB?
options: Zero-molecular
Unimolecular
Bimolecular
Termolecular

items.q: What is the rate law for step 3, 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO?
options: rate = k[NO₂]²
rate = k[NO₂]
rate = k[NO₃][NO]
rate = 2k[NO₂]

items.q: Which step is termolecular?
options: Step 1
Step 2
Step 3
Step 4

items.q: Why are termolecular steps like step 4 much less common than bimolecular steps?
options: Three particles rarely meet at the same instant
Three particles carry too much energy to stick together
Termolecular steps happen just in solids
Three particles are unable to line up in the right orientation

items.q: If [O₃] in step 1 is tripled, by what factor does the rate of step 1 change?
The overall reaction 2 H₂ + 2 NO → N₂ + 2 H₂O has the measured rate law rate = k[H₂][NO]². What can you conclude?
options: It is not one step: the orders differ from the coefficients
The reaction is a single step in which four molecules collide at once
The measured rate law is wrong, since the order in H₂ should be 2
Rate laws for overall reactions follow their coefficients

items.q: Which statements about elementary reactions are true? Select all that apply.
options: An elementary reaction happens in a single collision or event
The rate law of an elementary reaction follows from its coefficients
The rate law of an overall balanced equation follows from its coefficients
Most elementary reactions involve four or more particles

items.q: The elementary step NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂ has k = 1.8 × 10⁷ M⁻¹ s⁻¹ at a certain temperature. What is the rate, in M/s, when [NO] = 2.0 × 10⁻⁸ M and [O₃] = 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ M?

mistakes.why: Value: include [O₃] too: rate = k[NO][O₃].
Value: NO has coefficient 1, so it is first order here; do not square it.

items.q: An elementary step has the rate law rate = k[X]². Which equation could be that step?
options: 2 X → X₂
X → 2 Y
X + Y → XY
X₂ → 2 X

items.q: For the elementary step 2 NO₂ → NO₃ + NO, [NO₂] is halved at constant temperature. Predict each change.

In the gas phase, the elementary step H + Cl₂ → HCl + Cl is run in a container whose volume is then halved at constant temperature (no reaction during the squeeze). How does the rate of the step change?
options: It stays the same
It becomes 2 times as fast
It becomes 4 times as fast
It becomes 8 times as fast

items.q: Which elementary step has the rate law rate = k[NO][Cl₂]?
options: NO + Cl₂ → NOCl + Cl
2 NO + Cl₂ → 2 NOCl
NOCl + Cl → NO + Cl₂
2 NOCl → 2 NO + Cl₂

items.q: Which temperature is higher, and how does the graph show it?
options: T₂: its curve is flatter and spread to higher energies
T₁: its curve has the taller peak
T₁: more of its molecules have low energies
T₂: its curve holds more molecules in total

items.q: The reaction is faster at T₂. Which explanation uses the graph correctly?
options: At T₂ more of the molecules have 20 kJ/mol or more
At T₂ the activation energy is lower than 20 kJ/mol
At T₂ each molecule has at least 20 kJ/mol
At T₂ the molecules are smaller and fit together more easily

items.q: Raising the temperature makes molecules collide more often, and makes collisions more energetic. Which effect is larger for most reactions, and why?
options: The energy effect: the fraction above Ea grows fastest
The collision-frequency effect: faster molecules meet each other far more often
The two effects are about equal in size for most reactions
Neither: temperature changes the rate by changing the activation energy

items.q: On the graph, what represents the fraction of molecules that have enough energy to react at T₁?
options: The area under the T₁ curve to the right of 20 kJ/mol
The height of the T₁ peak
The energy at which the T₁ curve peaks
The area under the T₁ curve to the left of 20 kJ/mol

items.q: Which collision can lead to reaction, and why?
options: Collision 1: the Cl atom strikes the Cl end of NOCl
Collision 2: the Cl atom strikes the O end, which is more reactive
Both: each one has more than enough energy
Neither: Cl atoms need a third particle to react

items.q: Only a small fraction of collisions in a gas cause a reaction, even when the gas is hot. Which statements explain this? Select all that apply.
options: Many colliding pairs have less than the activation energy
Many collisions have the wrong orientation
Each molecule collides about once per second
Molecules lose a little mass each time they collide

items.q: The gas mixture is heated from 300 K to 320 K with the same container. Predict each change.

variables.name: Fraction of collisions with energy at or above Ea
Fraction of collisions with a suitable orientation

items.q: Which conditions must a collision meet to cause a reaction?
options: Enough energy and a suitable orientation
Energy of at least Ea, with any orientation
A suitable orientation, with any amount of energy
The two molecules have the same mass

items.q: Food spoils more slowly in a refrigerator. Which explanation uses the collision model correctly?
options: At lower temperature fewer collisions have enough energy to react
Cold temperatures raise the activation energy of the spoiling reactions
Cold molecules stop moving, so they no longer collide
Cold air contains fewer molecules of oxygen per liter

items.q: Two reactions run at the same temperature. Reaction X has Ea = 40 kJ/mol and reaction Y has Ea = 90 kJ/mol. Other factors are similar. Which statement is correct?
options: X is faster: more collisions reach its smaller Ea
Y is faster: its higher Ea gives each collision more energy
They have the same rate, since the temperature is the same
X is faster, since its molecules collide more often

items.q: A reaction in solution goes faster when the concentration of a reactant is raised, at constant temperature. Which part of the collision model explains this?
options: More particles per liter collide more often each second
Each collision has more energy at higher concentration
The activation energy falls at higher concentration
More particles per liter means each has the right orientation

items.q: For a reaction, 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ of all collisions have enough energy, and of those, 0.15 have a suitable orientation. In 1.0 L, 3.0 × 10³¹ collisions happen each second. How many effective collisions occur per second?

mistakes.why: Value: include the orientation factor too. Only 0.15 of the energetic collisions are oriented correctly.
Value: include the energy factor too. Only 2.0 × 10⁻⁵ of collisions have enough energy.

items.q: A student says, "Heating a reaction mixture lowers the activation energy, which is why it speeds up." Which response is best?
options: Ea is unchanged; more molecules now reach it
Correct: heating lowers Ea and makes collisions more frequent
Ea rises when heated, but collisions become more frequent
Heating speeds a reaction just by making molecules collide more often

items.q: A student grinds a solid reactant into a fine powder before adding it to a solution. According to the collision model, what changes?
options: More reactant particles are exposed, so collisions per second rise
Each collision now has more energy, so more of them react
The activation energy is lower for the small grains
The particles in the powder are oriented better

items.q: Two reactions have the same activation energy and are run at the same temperature and concentrations. In reaction 1 two small, round atoms combine; in reaction 2 a small molecule must hit one particular atom on a large molecule. Reaction 1 is much faster. Which explanation fits the collision model?
options: In reaction 2 most energetic collisions hit the wrong part of the large molecule
In reaction 2 the collisions carry too much energy, so the particles bounce apart
Large molecules collide with less kinetic energy at any temperature
Small atoms have a lower activation energy than large molecules

items.q: What is the activation energy of the reaction as written, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the energy of the transition state itself. Ea is the climb from the reactants: 150 − 40.
Value: you measured from the products. The forward Ea is measured from the reactants (40 kJ/mol).

items.q: What is the energy change for the reaction (products minus reactants), in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the products are lower than the reactants, so energy is released and the change is negative.
Value: that is the activation energy. The overall change compares the products with the reactants.

items.q: What is the activation energy for the reaction run in reverse, AB + C → A + BC, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: that is the forward Ea. Run in reverse, the reaction starts from the products (10 kJ/mol).
Sign: an activation energy is a climb, so it is positive.

items.q: What does the highest point of the curve represent?
options: The transition state, with bonds half broken and half formed
A stable molecule that can be collected
The products, which have the most energy
The average energy of the reactant molecules

items.q: Which reaction is faster, and why?
options: P, because its activation energy is smaller
Q, because it releases more energy
Q, because its products are lower in energy
They are equally fast, because they start at the same energy

items.q: Which statement describes the overall energy change of each reaction?
options: P absorbs energy (+25 kJ/mol); Q releases energy (−30 kJ/mol)
P releases energy (−25 kJ/mol); Q absorbs energy (+30 kJ/mol)
P absorbs 50 kJ/mol; Q absorbs 110 kJ/mol
Both release energy, since both start at 50 kJ/mol

items.q: A student claims, "Q releases energy, so it must be the faster reaction." Which evidence from the graph best refutes this?
options: Q's barrier is 110 kJ/mol, more than double P's 50 kJ/mol
Q's products are at 20 kJ/mol
P's products are at 75 kJ/mol
Both reactions start at 50 kJ/mol

items.q: Reaction P is warmed by 10 °C. Predict each change.
On an energy profile, the reactants are at 120 kJ/mol, the transition state at 185 kJ/mol and the products at 160 kJ/mol. Which statement is correct?
options: Ea = 65 kJ/mol; it absorbs 40 kJ/mol
Ea = 185 kJ/mol; it releases 40 kJ/mol
Ea = 25 kJ/mol; it absorbs 40 kJ/mol
Ea = 65 kJ/mol; it releases 40 kJ/mol

items.q: A one-step reaction releases 85 kJ/mol overall. Run in reverse, it has an activation energy of 210 kJ/mol. What is the activation energy of the reaction as written, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: the forward barrier is smaller when the reaction releases energy. Ea(forward) = Ea(reverse) − 85.
Value: that is the reverse barrier, climbed from the products.

items.q: Which statements about a reaction energy profile are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The activation energy is measured from the reactants up to the peak
The activation energy is measured from the products up to the peak
The peak is a stable substance that can be isolated
The vertical axis shows time

items.q: Why does a reaction with a very small activation energy usually happen quickly at room temperature?
options: Many collisions already have enough energy
Its products have less energy than its reactants
Its molecules collide more often than other molecules
Its transition state is lower than its products

items.q: For a one-step reaction, the forward activation energy is 48 kJ/mol and the reverse activation energy is 75 kJ/mol. What is the overall energy change, products minus reactants, in kJ/mol?

mistakes.why: Sign: the reverse barrier is larger, so the products are lower than the reactants and the change is negative.
Value: subtract the barriers, do not add them: 48 − 75.

items.q: A reaction releases a lot of energy but does not happen when its reactants are mixed at room temperature. Which explanation is consistent with its energy profile?
options: Its Ea is large, so few collisions react
Its products are higher in energy than its reactants
Its transition state is lower than its reactants
It has no activation energy, so it does not start

items.q: Two one-step reactions have the same energy change, −40 kJ/mol. Reaction 1 has Ea = 30 kJ/mol and reaction 2 has Ea = 90 kJ/mol. How do their transition states compare?
options: Reaction 2's transition state is 60 kJ/mol higher above its reactants
They are at the same height, since the energy changes are equal
Reaction 1's transition state is higher, since its Ea is smaller
Neither reaction has a transition state, since both release energy
